lesson.title: Rugged Individualism Meets Hard Times: Hoover's Response to the Depression
lesson.summary: President Herbert Hoover took more federal action against the Depression than many people remember, but his commitment to voluntary cooperation, limited direct relief, and balanced budgets proved inadequate to the scale of the crisis.
lesson.body:
Herbert Hoover was elected president in 1928, defeating Democrat Al Smith, and took office in March 1929, just months before the stock market crash. The choice seemed almost ironic in hindsight, since Hoover had built his reputation as an exceptionally capable administrator, having led major relief efforts for Belgium during World War I and served effectively as Secretary of Commerce under Presidents Harding and Coolidge.

Hoover's guiding philosophy was what he called rugged individualism: a belief that voluntary cooperation among business, labor, local government, and private charity, not direct federal handouts to individuals, should carry the nation through hard times. He feared that a government dole would sap Americans' self-reliance and character. In practice, this meant Hoover urged, rather than required, business leaders to maintain wages and employment levels, and he leaned on organized, voluntary efforts before turning to more direct federal intervention.

Hoover did take real action, more than his reputation as a do-nothing president often suggests. He had already created the Federal Farm Board in 1929, even before the crash, to help stabilize falling crop prices. In January 1932, he established the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, which extended loans to banks, railroads, and other large institutions in the hope that stabilizing them would eventually help the broader economy recover, an approach built on the assumption that aid would trickle down to ordinary workers and families. In June 1930, he signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, intending to protect American industry and farmers from foreign competition, though as discussed earlier this instead provoked retaliation abroad and worsened the global trade contraction. In 1932, he also signed the Revenue Act, which raised taxes substantially in an effort to balance the federal budget, a choice most economists today view as exactly the wrong move during a severe economic contraction.

These measures proved far too limited given the scale of the disaster. By 1933, national unemployment had climbed to roughly one in four workers. Hoover's reluctance to provide direct relief to suffering individuals and families, combined with his insistence on balanced budgets even as the economy collapsed, left millions of Americans feeling abandoned by their government. His name became attached, mockingly and bitterly, to the visible symbols of the era's hardship, the shantytowns known as Hoovervilles that are the subject of the next chapter, and his standing with the public would soon suffer an even sharper blow in the confrontation known as the Bonus Army.
